rv.q: Wrapped in such a garment, Dring's play itself can sometimes feel a bit like a junior wrestler attempting to wear a tsuna, the ceremonial 30-pound belt awarded to sumo wrestlers when they reach yokozuna, the sport's highest rank.

But what’s authentic and respectful may not always feel satisfying emotionally, and “Sumo,” a Ma-Yi Theater Company and La Jolla Playhouse production that opened Wednesday at the Public Theater, rarely rises to the dramatic heights it seeks.
The play is a solid contender, but it doesn't have quite enough surprising moves to rise to the level of champion.
Whatever the script's shortcomings, SUMO gives us a glimpse of a world most of us wouldn't otherwise see.
Sumo is an informative and lovingly detailed look into the life of a modern-day sumo wrestler that incorporates the universally accessible theme of society's relationship with masculinity.

Otherwise, Dring stays on well-intentioned, dramatically inert message, juxtaposing the toxic masculinity that’s distressingly prevalent in the sumo ring (dohyō), a sacred space women aren’t even allowed to enter, against forms of manliness that are gentle, supportive, and loving.
One of the more entertaining Off-Broadway shows this season.
Sumo is on firmer ground when it focuses on the sport itself.
'Sumo' is a compelling exploration of dedication, honor, tradition
